Welcome

For twenty years, operational risk quantification was driven largely by internal models for regulatory capital. Those models are no longer required for regulatory capital. But the need for quantification has not disappeared — on the contrary, it has grown across new risk types and a wider range of applications.

Economic capital, stress testing, operational resilience, risk appetite and insurance all require a quantitative view of operational risk. However, these applications are often addressed separately, with their own assumptions, methods and numbers.

Rare but severe events play a particular role in economic capital, where they largely determine the amount of capital required. But they are also critical to stress testing, operational resilience, risk appetite and insurance. Scenario analysis can therefore provide a common foundation across these applications.

But a scenario narrative is not sufficient for this purpose. A structured loss-generation mechanism is needed to describe how the risk can crystallise and unfold. This is precisely what MSTAR and the XOI method are designed to do, and what this guide sets out to explain.

MSTAR and the XOI method start from the structure of the risk itself: what is exposed, what can happen to it, what consequences may follow, and which drivers influence each part of the mechanism. Once that structure is explicit, the same model can be used and interrogated in different ways for different purposes.

The following pages explain the methodology, show how it is applied to real operational risks, describe the MSTAR Library and its business uses, and set out our approach to validation and AI-assisted challenge. The final section lets you try the approach yourself.

Although this approach may be more demanding upfront, it brings considerable simplification. Once the risk is structured properly, the same foundation can support multiple applications and answer different operational-risk questions consistently.

MSTAR Methodology
Section 1

Why MSTAR?

Operational risk is now assessed for multiple purposes. ICAAP, stress testing, CCAR, risk appetite, operational resilience, scenario analysis and insurance all require a quantitative view of the same underlying risks. Yet these requirements are still frequently addressed separately. Different exercises use different methods, assumptions and metrics, producing multiple views of risks that ultimately arise from the same operations. As new requirements emerge, another analysis is added rather than derived from a common understanding of how the risk works.

This fragmentation has deep roots. Operational risk has long been the poor relation of quantitative risk management. Credit and market risk are modelled through the mechanisms that generate loss; operational risk, for the most part, has been modelled through the losses themselves. The main difficulty was not mathematical but conceptual: what exactly does exposure mean in operational risk?

In credit and market risk, monetary exposure provides a natural starting point. A loan defines the amount exposed to default; a market position defines the amount whose value is sensitive to market movements. Quantification can therefore begin with the amount exposed and model how loss arises — EAD, PD and LGD in credit; position, sensitivity and shock in market risk. No bank models its credit risk simply by fitting a distribution to past write-offs.

Operational risk lacks this natural monetary exposure. For an error, disruption, fraud or conduct event, there is no monetary amount at risk before the event occurs. One response is to define exposure in non-monetary terms and model how events acting on a non-financial exposed resource generate financial consequences. The other is to bypass exposure and model losses directly.

Historically, the industry largely followed the second route. Basel II encouraged loss-based internal models, loss data became increasingly available, and defining operational risk exposure was difficult. The Loss Distribution Approach was a natural consequence: instead of modelling the conditions through which severe losses arise, models fitted statistical distributions capable of generating sufficiently extreme loss values.

But a distribution of outcomes is not a model of how risk works. It cannot naturally show how changes in activity, processes, controls or external conditions alter the risk. More importantly today, it provides little common structure from which different risk-management questions can be answered. A capital number, a resilience assessment, a risk-appetite measure and a stress test may all concern the same underlying risk, yet they can end up being constructed independently.

The end of Basel internal-model capital requirements did not remove the need for operational risk quantification. It exposed the broader need: a common representation of risk that can support many different applications.

MSTAR starts from that representation. It defines operational risk exposure explicitly and models the mechanisms through which exposures, events and impacts combine to produce loss. Once those mechanisms are represented, the same structural model can be interrogated in different ways — for capital, stress testing, resilience, risk appetite, scenario analysis, insurance or future requirements that may not yet exist.

The questions can change. The model of how the risk works remains the common foundation to meet every requirement.

Section 2

The MSTAR Approach

The MSTAR methodology started with an idea that was not ours.

Nearly twenty years ago, while working with a large French bank to build its AMA model, its Head of Operational Risk decided to train all operational risk managers in the Associate in Risk Management (ARM) programme developed by The Institutes. She wanted the consultants working with her teams to share the same approach, so we took the same eighteen-month programme.

ARM drew on the work of early risk management thinkers, including George L. Head, who played an important role in professional risk management education at the Insurance Institute of America.

One of the foundations of ARM particularly caught our attention: the triplet Peril – Object – Consequence. The Peril is the event that may happen. The Object is what is exposed to it. The Consequence is what results when the two meet.

While ARM used this decomposition primarily as a qualitative risk management framework, we set out to design a quantitative version of it.

The Risk Quantification Model

To make the ARM triplet quantitative, we translated its three elements into quantities that could be modelled: eXposure, Occurrence and Impact, or XOI.

Exposure is the set of objects, or resources, exposed to the adverse event. Occurrence is the probability that this event occurs for a particular exposed object. Impact is what the consequences are when it does.

These three elements cannot always be quantified precisely. Each can be uncertain, and their combination produces a distribution of potential losses. They are also influenced by risk drivers, which may affect one or several of them at the same time.

This is the break described in Section 1. Loss is not inferred from a curve fitted to past losses; it is generated by a mechanism that starts from Exposure and combines Occurrence and Impact. What EAD, PD and LGD do for credit risk, Exposure, Occurrence and Impact do for operational risk: they decompose the mechanism through which exposure becomes loss.

The Risk Management Model

Another important contribution of ARM was to organise risk management around three pillars: Diagnosis, Reduction and Financing. We also wanted our approach to reflect the Reduction and Financing aspects. To do this, we built what we called the Risk Management Influence Diagram.

An influence diagram is a graphical representation of how uncertain quantities, decisions and outcomes interact. In our case, it shows how the quantified risk model connects to the actions available to the risk manager.

The central part of the diagram describes the XOI loss-generation mechanism.

The diagram then extends the model to risk management. Risk can be acted upon through two levers, each carrying its own cost.

Reduction works upstream. It acts on the risk drivers – through process improvement, controls, resilience, training and other measures – to reduce Exposure, Occurrence or Impact. This effort consumes resources, represented by the Cost of Reduction.

Transfer works downstream. It acts on losses that would otherwise be retained through insurance, transferring part of their financial consequences to an insurer at a Cost of Transfer.

Reduction lowers the risk itself, while Transfer changes how its financial consequences are borne. The losses that remain with the bank form the Cost of Retained Losses. Together, these three components form the Risk Cost: the total cost of the risk to the organisation.

Risk Cost = Cost of Reduction + Cost of Retained Losses + Cost of Transfer

The objective is therefore not simply to minimise losses, but to find the combination of mitigation and transfer that minimises the total Risk Cost.

XOI not only solves the problem of defining exposure for operational risk; by connecting quantification to reduction and transfer, it also bridges the gap between risk quantification and risk management.

Section 3

Analysing Operational Risk with XOI

The real shift in operational risk measurement and management comes from defining its exposure portfolio: not a portfolio of financial assets, but of productive resources – people, systems, suppliers, platforms and even products.

Operational risk can then be seen as the occurrence of an adverse event affecting one of these resources. This puts operational risk on the same conceptual footing as other risk types: start from what is exposed, then model what may happen to it and the loss that may result.

The best way to see how this works is to start with a few concrete risks. We take three examples and look more closely at the definition of X, O and I, and at the factors that influence them. These factors are represented in dependency graphs, with relationships that may be deterministic or probabilistic. The models shown are illustrative.

Risk = Resource × Event
What is exposed? × What can happen to it?

Example 1: Rogue Trading

A trader builds and conceals a large directional and unprotected position, aiming to create large profits once the market moves in favour of the position. The position is detected a few weeks later, but unwinding it generates a large loss as the market has moved against it.

Example 2: Cyber Attack

This scenario considers a cyber-attack that makes a critical application unavailable and disrupts operations. The attack targets one of the bank's critical services; as the service is disrupted, the bank incurs revenue loss, client compensation and remediation costs.

Example 3: Key Supplier Failure

This scenario considers disruption of a key supplier in two situations: financial default, requiring a permanent switch to another supplier, and technical failure, where the supplier cannot provide the service for a period exceeding the contractual agreement.

A broader view: rethinking operational risk taxonomy

The same XOI logic can be applied across very different types of operational risk. The table below shows how Exposure, Occurrence and Impact can be identified for risks across the Basel categories.

Basel categoryRiskExposureOccurrenceImpact
Internal fraudRogue TradingTradersGoing roguePosition × market change
External fraudCyber Attack on Critical ServiceImportant Business ServicesDDoS or MalwareRevenue Loss + Client Compensation + Fine
Employment PracticesEmployee Class ActionEmployeesClass actionSettlement × N employees
Business PracticesMis-sellingProductsCollective challengeDetriment × N clients
Damage to Physical AssetsNatural DisasterBuildingsNatural disasterBuilding + business
Business DisruptionSupplier FailureKey suppliersBankruptcy / disruptionReplacement + business
ExecutionTrading ErrorTradesErrorAmount × market change

The relevant unit of exposure depends on the risk being modelled. It may be a person, a service, a product, a building, a supplier or a transaction.

If operational risk is understood as an adverse Event affecting an exposed Resource and leading to Consequences, it becomes natural to build the risk taxonomy by combining a taxonomy of exposed resources with a taxonomy of events.

This approach helps avoid two common shortcomings of taxonomies defined as flat lists. First, such taxonomies may place at the same level concepts of very different kinds: causes or aggravating factors, risk events, activities or resources exposed to those events, and sometimes even their consequences.

Second, they may lose sight of a very simple principle: risk is the possibility of a loss. A useful test is therefore to ask whether a risk category could reasonably be used to describe an actual loss event.

Consider a few categories commonly found in operational risk frameworks:

CategoryWhat it actually describes
Supervisory OversightCause or aggravating factor of potential conduct events
Business ContinuityCause or aggravating factor of potential disruption events (if inadequate)
Project RiskActivity or resource exposed to risk events
People RiskResource exposed to risk events

These are all relevant concepts for risk management. But they cannot be the name of a loss event. A loss database may contain events described as Fraud, Trading Error, Data Breach or Mis-selling. It would be difficult to imagine a loss event described as Supervisory Oversight or People Risk.

These shortcomings are avoided when building on the two principles derived from XOI.

Principle 1: A risk is the occurrence of an unwanted event on a resource. There is something exposed to risk – a person, a system, a building, a product, an activity; and there is an event that may affect it. The event-resource combination must be capable of producing a loss.

Principle 2: A risk is the possibility of a loss. This also provides a practical consistency test: a properly defined risk category should be capable of describing an event that could appear in a loss database.

Taken together, these two principles lead naturally to a two-dimensional operational risk taxonomy: Resource × Event. The Resource taxonomy answers one question: what is exposed? The Event taxonomy answers another: what can happen to it? A risk is defined by the intersection of the two.

Resources are the productive resources used by the bank to conduct its business: people, third parties, material and intangible assets, and banking activities. These are the objects exposed to operational risk events. Only combinations in which an event can directly affect a resource correspond to risks.

Direct and indirect exposure: the taxonomy identifies the resource directly exposed to the event. Other resources may be affected indirectly as consequences unfold. For example, a disruption may directly affect an IT system and, as a consequence, disrupt the banking activities that depend on it.

This approach does not make causes, controls or consequences disappear. They remain essential to risk analysis and risk management. It simply gives them their proper place in the risk model instead of mixing them within the taxonomy itself.

The complete MSTAR taxonomy extends the Resource × Event matrix into hierarchical classifications of productive resources and operational events. The image below is included simply to show that the framework is not just theoretical: it can be developed into a concrete taxonomy:

  • Cells with an R indicate a Risk
  • Cells with an S indicate Risk with one or more Scenarios, i.e. Major Risks (see MSTAR Library of Scenarios)
  • Cells in yellow indicate an indirect impact
  • Cells in grey indicate an absence of possible or significant risk

A structured taxonomy imposes a discipline: a risk category must correspond to a meaningful Resource × Event combination. New concerns cannot therefore be added simply because they have become important. This may appear rigid. What happens, for example, when a new concern such as AI Risk emerges?

This is where Risk Themes come in. A Risk Theme groups together Resource × Event combinations that are relevant to a particular concern at a given point in time. AI Risk, for example, does not correspond to a single cell in the taxonomy. AI may itself be an exposed resource in Model Risk, as an AI model is a new type of model. It may also act as a driver across several event types, increasing the likelihood or impact of cyber attacks, fraud, errors or improper business practices.

This makes the framework both stable and flexible. The taxonomy does not need to be redesigned whenever a new concern becomes important. The taxonomy provides the stable structure; Risk Themes provide flexible, cross-cutting views of that structure.

MSTAR in Practice
Section 4

MSTAR Library of Scenarios

A reference scenario is a complete XOI model, not a narrative template.
It combines a structured loss-generation mechanism with a reference quantification. Bank-specific parameters are adapted to the institution; external parameters provide reusable reference points.

The MSTAR Library contains generic, stylised reference scenarios, informed by our experience across our projects and by the analysis of more than 2,500 significant operational loss cases. Each scenario is also quantified for a fictional reference institution, the MSTAR Bank. This provides reference values for the drivers. Some reflect the external environment, such as the probability of specific events or the level of regulatory fines relative to revenue. Others are specific to the bank, such as its exposures, activities or controls.

The MSTAR Library covers seven families of operational risk. Each scenario is a full XOI model --- exposure, occurrence, impact and their drivers --- not a description or a checklist. Each carries a short code used across the Platform.

Reference Quantification

Each scenario is quantified for the MSTAR Bank, providing a complete example of how the model can be populated. Some parameters are specific to the reference bank, such as its exposures, activities or controls. Others reflect the external environment and can be used as reference parameters when the scenario is adapted to another institution.

These reusable parameters are quantified from public studies, industry analyses and operational loss events, depending on the nature of the risk. Conduct scenarios provide a good example. In many of them, the wrongdoing itself generates improper revenue: excess fees from overcharging, excess margins from anti-competitive practices, or revenue from products that were mis-sold. The resulting fine, settlement or compensation can therefore be related to the revenue associated with the improper practice.

For these scenarios, we analyse as comprehensively as possible the publicly available cases in order to estimate a distribution of impact intensity --- the ratio between the financial loss and the relevant revenue.

This is also why monitoring operational risk events matters. New cases need to be identified and classified not only within broad Basel categories, but within the specific scenarios whose parameters they can inform.

Section 5

Business Cases with MSTAR

Once a structured scenario has been built, the same model can serve many purposes. It can be reused across regulatory and capital applications as well as internal risk management. This section reviews the main use cases. They fall into the two families introduced in Section 1: regulatory and capital applications, and internal risk management.

Regulatory and capital

Economic capital (ICAAP). Scenarios are created, quantified and aggregated. MSTAR includes a dedicated aggregation module in which the dependencies between scenarios are specified explicitly. The resulting portfolio distribution allows economic capital to be calculated at a given percentile. The Enterprise Model combines individual scenarios into a portfolio view, so capital can be assessed at group level rather than scenario by scenario.

Stress testing. Structured scenarios can be used for regulatory stress testing, including exercises such as CCAR in the US, in two main ways. The first is to select scenarios from the portfolio and assume that the events have occurred. The second is to define a common stress and translate it into the relevant assumptions or drivers of each affected scenario. A geopolitical stress, for example, may affect cyber scenarios, market-activity scenarios and some financial-crime scenarios. Because each scenario is structured, the stress can be applied differently depending on how it affects the underlying risk mechanism.

From Dependencies to Correlations

Aggregating operational risk scenarios requires assumptions about dependencies. Rather than asking users to estimate correlations directly, MSTAR starts by identifying the dependency paths that may connect scenarios. Each scenario owner assesses whether the occurrence of a scenario may deteriorate an environmental stress factor — relations with clients or regulators, human resources, and so on — and, conversely, whether deterioration in one of these factors may make the scenario more likely. Combining these assessments across all scenarios, MSTAR identifies dependency paths that can be translated into a correlation matrix, which can then be reviewed and adjusted before the portfolio simulation is run.

This reflects the same principle used throughout MSTAR: start from the mechanisms rather than from a purely technical estimate.

Operational resilience. Operational resilience is fundamentally a risk management concern, but it has increasingly become subject to regulatory requirements, notably through DORA in the EU.

Here the focus shifts from the probability of a disruption to its consequences once it has occurred. Structured scenarios are particularly useful because the event is modelled on a specific resource or service. The impact therefore depends not only on the nature of the event, but also on the resource affected, the duration and timing of the disruption, and the conditions under which recovery takes place.

Outages can have very different consequences depending on which service is interrupted and when it occurs. By making these elements explicit, structured scenarios support resilience assessments resource by resource and service by service.

A Structured Approach to Operational Resilience

Rather than assessing operational resilience scenario by scenario, using a collection of "severe but plausible" events, MSTAR supports a more systematic approach.

The starting point is to identify the bank's Important Business Services, the revenues associated with them and the transactions they process. The revenues are decomposed into categories that react differently to a disruption, e.g. recurring interest income, interest income from new business, fees earned on existing balances and fees generated by transaction flows. Transaction volumes and values provide a basis for estimating possible customer compensation.

A dependency graph is then built to link each IBS to the key resources on which it depends. This graph can be used to create specific instances of the relevant MSTAR scenarios when a particular resource is disrupted: Supplier Failure, Data Centre Disruption, Cyber Attack on Critical Service, Critical Service Disruption, Natural Disaster, etc. The scenario can then be simulated, taking into account the remaining uncertainties, such as the duration and severity of the disruption.

A disruption may also increase other operational risks. A major outage, for example, may make processing errors or fraud more likely. Rather than building all these possible ramifications into one large resilience scenario, MSTAR uses its scenario dependency framework to connect the initial disruption to the other scenarios it may affect. The combined simulation can therefore capture the wider consequences of the disruption while keeping each individual scenario simple and reusable.

Risk management

Structured Scenario Analysis was designed as both a risk quantification and a risk management tool, as discussed earlier. But it has an important by-product: building the model is itself a risk management exercise. Defining its structure and searching for the data needed to quantify it forces the risk to be examined in detail, and can reveal unexpected gaps that were not apparent from the initial qualitative assessment.

Risk appetite and limits. Risk appetite deserves separate treatment because quantitative approaches to operational risk appetite remain less standardised than the applications above. It is still often expressed through qualitative statements and indicator limits that are difficult to connect to an overall view of potential losses.

Using structured scenarios, it becomes possible to build a quantitative framework in three stages: Setting, Allocation and Monitoring:

  • Setting. Risk appetite remains a management decision. Quantification provides the risk profile on which that decision can be based, but the decision itself cannot be automated. Management defines zones on the risk distribution: what is expected, what is within tolerance, what requires active management, and what is out of appetite.
  • Allocation. The group-wide appetite is allocated across risk types using structured scenarios, and across business or assessment units using appropriate allocation keys.
  • Monitoring. Realised losses consume part of the allocated appetite, while structured scenarios are recalculated as exposures and risk conditions change. The revised prospective risk profile is then compared with the appetite remaining for the rest of the period.
A Simple Risk Appetite Example

At the beginning of the year, a bank allocates €200m of risk appetite to IT and information security, measured at the 90th percentile. A major incident then causes €50m of losses, leaving €150m of risk capacity for the remainder of the year.

At the same time, ransomware risk increases. The relevant scenarios are recalibrated and rerun. The revised 90th percentile of potential losses for the rest of the year is now €180m.

The bank is therefore out of appetite: it has already lost €50m and still faces €180m of potential losses at the selected probability level. Management can act before any further loss occurs — through additional mitigation, reallocation of risk appetite, or both.

Business change analysis. A What-if analysis changes one or more assumptions in a scenario to assess the effect on risk. A stress test applies a common adverse condition across the scenarios for which it is relevant. Business change analysis uses the same principle, but starts from a planned change in the business rather than from an adverse external condition: rapid growth, a merger, entry into a new country, or a major change in activity.

Because the scenarios are structured, the effects of the change can be translated into changes in Exposure, drivers or other relevant assumptions across the portfolio. The resulting risk profile can therefore be assessed before the decision is taken.

Insurance and risk transfer. MSTAR includes an insurance module that connects the losses generated by the scenarios to an insurance programme. The programme may contain several policies or covers, each described by its characteristics: deductibles, limits, share of cover, probability of non-coverage and other coverage conditions.

The simulation is then run with the insurance programme in place. For each simulated loss, MSTAR determines the amount retained by the bank and the amount transferred to the insurer. The resulting distributions make it possible to assess whether the programme is appropriately calibrated and to compare alternative structures, limits or deductibles.

The analysis can be performed for the full insurance programme or for a particular policy, such as cyber insurance. It therefore provides a quantitative basis for designing the programme and discussing its terms with insurers.

In the Risk Cost framework introduced earlier, the module also makes it possible to compare the Cost of Transfer with the losses that remain with the bank.

Supporting the Business Cases: in-house Library of Scenarios

The MSTAR Library of Scenarios can be brought in-house. With the Enterprise (on-premise) platform, it is installed inside the bank and fully customised – its scenarios, data and assumptions maintained internally, and enriched over time as the bank's own experience feeds back into it.

Throughout, the split is the one used elsewhere: the Library holds the structured knowledge – scenarios, indicators, assumptions and the events behind them; while MSTAR stays a pure modelling and calculation engine.

Section 6

Model Validation

Model Validation

MSTAR Structured Scenarios have been used by financial institutions in regulatory processes and model submissions accepted by authorities in the EU, UK and US, including for regulatory capital, economic capital and stress testing. However, each institution must conduct its own independent validation.

Validation has to be adapted to what a structured scenario is. The events addressed are generally rare, so the models are not data-driven, and validation techniques designed for models calibrated on historical loss data are therefore of limited relevance. As the old saying goes, all models are wrong, but some are useful: the aim is not to prove that a scenario is true, but to assess whether it is fit for its intended purpose.

The Federal Reserve's revised Model Risk Management guidance, SR 26-2, states that model validation evaluates whether models perform as expected, and that the nature and rigor of validation should reflect the model's approach, use and materiality. It also states that effective model development begins with a clear statement of purpose. The first step, therefore, is to define what the structured scenario is intended to be used for.

For validation purposes, a structured scenario can be broken down into five components, each requiring a different form of review or validation.

The XOI methodology. The XOI methodology provides a general framework for representing operational risk. Validation therefore focuses on how this framework is applied to each particular risk. For example, XOI assumes that exposed units are independent given the drivers; this assumption must be reasonable for the risk being modelled.

The calculation engine. The engine implements the XOI methodology using Monte Carlo simulation and Bayesian networks. In principle, it only needs to be validated once — for instance by replicating it in an external tool and comparing the results. To make this possible, MSTAR can export a script equivalent to any structured scenario in Python, R or Matlab.

The loss-generation mechanism. This describes how the risk occurs and unfolds for an exposed unit. It is validated by independent business experts (organised, for example, as a challenge panel) who assess whether the mechanism is reasonable and whether all material impacts have been captured.

The quantifiers. Each driver is quantified using one of four main sources: internal business data, internal loss data, external loss data, or expert judgement. The validation approach depends on the source. Data-based quantifiers are subject to data-quality validation, while judgement-based quantifiers are challenged by independent experts.

The resulting distribution. Running the engine on the structure and the quantifiers produces a distribution of potential losses. It is an empirical distribution — no curve is fitted on top of it. The result can then be challenged by comparing its loss frequency and key percentiles with expert judgement or external data.

The pattern is consistent throughout: structural and judgement-based assumptions are challenged by independent experts, while data-based assumptions are subject to data-quality validation. The calculation engine can be validated independently of individual scenarios, while the application of the XOI methodology is assessed for each risk. Because every assumption is explicit, validation can focus on how the model is built, not only on the distribution it produces.

Section 7

MSTAR Recognition

Twenty years, the largest banks, external recognition

The XOI method is not new. Elseware was founded in 1993. Its work began with an earlier generation of neural networks applied to credit and market risk, before moving to Bayesian networks. XOI grew out of that work and was introduced in 2006. Since then, it has been used by some of the largest banks in the world.

Its first uses were regulatory. Some major international banks adopted the method in their Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) models because they saw value in a more structured representation of operational risk, even though the approach was still unconventional. Those models were subsequently approved by regulators. Others used XOI to challenge their internal models at the request of regulators. As the regulatory landscape changed, XOI continued to be used for other purposes: to build CCAR submissions, to revise operational risk taxonomies, and more broadly to rethink how operational risk was approached.

That continuity is the point. When the AMA was withdrawn, XOI remained relevant because its value was never only regulatory. It was methodological: a way to understand, quantify and manage risk that outlasted the capital framework for which it had first been adopted.

External recognition

The ABA/MSTAR Cyber Risk Modelling Project received Risk.net's Industry Initiative of the Year award in 2020. Led by the American Bankers Association (ABA) and built on MSTAR Structured Scenario Analysis, the initiative brought together major US banks to develop common cyber-risk scenarios and benchmark their assumptions and results.

In 2020-2021, ORX, the international operational risk association, ran an industry initiative to explore structured scenarios based on Bayesian networks, in collaboration with Elseware. The project brought together banks and insurers to develop and test structured approaches to operational risk. In its public report, ORX concluded: "We believe that there is huge merit for the use of structured scenarios for operational risk management."

Aviva also used an Elseware-developed Bayesian network approach, derived from operational risk modelling, to aggregate climate risks and calculate its Climate VaR. This methodology was incorporated into Aviva's climate-related financial disclosures. Aviva's climate reporting subsequently received Environmental Finance's 2021 TCFD Report of the Year award, and PwC's Building Public Trust Award for Climate Change Reporting in both 2021 and 2022.

Section 8

MSTAR and AI

We use AI primarily to challenge scenarios rather than build them.

A scenario is first structured explicitly in MSTAR: exposures, events, impacts and their drivers, together with the data and assumptions required to quantify them. AI is then used to test those assumptions against external evidence, identify relevant information and help the modeller decide whether an estimate should be retained or revised.

From information to evidence

The process starts with specialised search agents. Some monitor news and recent events; others search studies, industry reports, regulatory publications and similar sources. Their role is not simply to retrieve documents, but to extract factual information that may be relevant to a specific modelling assumption.

Those facts are stored in a Fact Base, together with their sources and context. This creates a reusable evidence layer: the same facts can support many scenarios and modelling questions rather than being gathered again for each one.

For example, in a cyber scenario, agents specialised in surveys and industry reports may collect information on the frequency of major cyber incidents — across the financial sector, within European banks, or within another relevant peer group. Separately, agents specialised in news may collect comparable events to provide evidence on a different indicator, such as the duration of service disruption following a cyberattack.

Challenging the indicators

The next layer consists of specialised query agents that use the Fact Base to challenge individual model indicators. A probability query agent can examine evidence relevant to the occurrence rate of an event; an intensity query agent can focus on a driver of impact, such as the duration of a disruption.

The question presented to AI is therefore deliberately narrow. Instead of asking: "What is the probability of a major cyber outage?" the model may ask: "Our scenario assumes that an outage of this type occurs once every 20 years. What evidence supports or contradicts that assumption?" Or, for impact: "The scenario assumes that 40% of transactions are disrupted during the first six hours. Is that consistent with evidence from comparable incidents?"

AI analyses the available evidence, identifies relevant facts, assesses whether they support or contradict the current estimate, and documents the reasoning behind the challenge. The modeller then decides whether the assumption should be retained, revised or investigated further.

The result is a simple chain.

AI improves the evidence available to the modeller and makes the challenge more systematic. MSTAR remains the explicit modelling and simulation engine: assumptions, distributions, dependencies and calculations stay visible and auditable. Nothing in the calculation becomes a black box.

Structure first, challenge second, decide third

This order is not incidental. AI can only challenge systematically what is explicit. A narrative scenario leaves its scope and assumptions loosely defined, and the challenge can easily drift from one risk mechanism to another as evidence is gathered. A structured scenario fixes the exposure, the loss-generating mechanism and the underlying assumptions, so the problem itself does not change while it is being challenged. Structure is what makes the challenge focused, traceable and systematic.

This is why our approach is AI in the loop, not human in the loop. The human modeller owns the process and the decisions; AI participates at the stages where it is most useful — searching large volumes of information, extracting relevant facts, comparing evidence with assumptions and documenting the challenge. It does not generate an opaque scenario for a human to approve after the fact.

For the same reason, AI here is a tool for the modeller, not a product for the end-user. The output is an explicit MSTAR model whose assumptions and calculations can be reviewed independently of the AI that helped develop and challenge them.

More detail on the evolution of operational risk scenario analysis is set out in a recent Risk.net white paper.
Section 9

FAQ

Common questions and objections
What is a scenario, according to this method?

It is not one instance of a possible occurrence of the risk. It is a generator of possible situations. If you have already worked with single-point scenarios, they remain very useful – to identify the drivers, and to discuss the plausible ranges of the assumptions.

Is this a model?

Yes. It is a representation of reality – of how things could happen and unfold. But there is no "true distribution" that we are trying to approach.

Isn't this just expert judgement?

Every operational risk method rests on judgement – including the LDA. The LDA looks objective because it starts from loss data, but judgement is everywhere in it, only hidden: where the collection threshold sits, what counts as a single loss event, how old losses are scaled, which severity distribution is chosen, how the tail is fitted, what dependencies are assumed. Each of these choices moves the capital number, and none is dictated by the data. As an illustration, under an LDA, merging two loss events into one - or splitting one into two - can change the capital figure, yet nothing in the data says which is correct.

The structured approach does not remove judgement; it cannot. What it does is make every assumption explicit, so it can be challenged – by experts, and against data where data exists. Subjectivity that is visible and documented is safer than subjectivity buried in data treatment.

How is this different from the LDA?

The LDA fits a distribution to the historical record of losses. The structured approach models the mechanism that produces losses — exposure, occurrence and impact — and lets the distribution emerge from it. One reasons about outcomes; the other reasons about causes. This is the shift described in Section 1: model the risk, not the loss.

Can this be validated using loss data?

Losses cannot be predicted. A risk model can only be validated by backtesting that the projected metric — a VaR, for instance — is not exceeded. For models that use expert opinion, backtesting would require being able to reconstitute past expert opinions, which is not feasible.

Can this be validated at all?

Yes. Each piece of information can be challenged by experts and against existing data, where data exists. The loss distribution can be checked for consistency with internal and external losses. An insurance premium is another possible consistency check — though a consistency check, not a validation.

What about model risk, auditors and regulators?

Because the assumptions are explicit, the model can be reviewed on its process rather than only on its output. A reviewer can ask whether the scenario was decomposed correctly, whether data was used where available, and whether each assumption is documented and defensible — rather than only debating the final loss number. This is precisely what makes a structured scenario easier to audit than a single loss estimate.

Do I need a lot of data to start?

No. The method combines data where it exists with structured judgement where it does not. That is exactly the situation for severe operational risk, where history is thinnest — and where a purely data-driven approach has the least to say.

Do I need to be a statistician?

No. The model is built in business terms — the resources exposed, what can happen to them, what it would cost. The engine handles the computation. The work of the risk manager is to describe the mechanism, not to fit a distribution.

Is this still useful now that AMA capital is gone?

Yes. The need did not disappear with the capital rule. ICAAP, stress testing and operational resilience still require a defensible view of severe risk, and internal risk management — risk appetite, prospective analysis, insurance — relies on the same models. Section 5 sets out these uses.

Where does AI fit in?

AI does not produce the scenario and does not replace judgement. Its role is to challenge: to search for evidence, to assess whether it supports or contradicts the assumptions, and to document the reasoning. This works only because the scenario is structured. Section 8 covers this in more detail.

How can MSTAR models be validated?

Model validation is addressed at several distinct levels — methodology, calculation engine, loss-generation mechanism, quantification assumptions and the resulting loss distribution. See Section 6, Model Validation.

Why are exposed units assumed independent?

They are not assumed independent outright. They are assumed independent given the drivers. The dependence between units is carried by the shared drivers: when a common driver moves — a stress condition, an external factor — it moves the affected units together. This is what lets common stress be represented explicitly, without correlating everything by hand.

Why Monte-Carlo simulation?

A structured scenario has far too many possible combinations to compute exactly — each exposed unit may or may not be hit, and each impact may vary. Monte-Carlo simulation draws a large number of possible situations at random and, from them, reconstructs the distribution of potential losses.

Section 10

Now, try it!

Two ways to start
Adapt a reference scenario — fast first quantification · Build from scratch — full control of the model

You have seen what the method does. This section shows the whole thing in action --- one complete scenario, built from scratch in MSTAR, from the first analysis to simulation and What-if. It is the shortest way to understand what you can do yourself.

It is also a different route from the Library wizard in Section 3. There, you adapt a ready-made scenario to your bank in a few steps. Here, you build a model from the ground up. Fast start on one side, full control on the other.

Try a scenario template

Each scenario comes with a wizard that adapts it to your institution. You don't need to build anything: you take the reference model and replace the MSTAR Bank's default values with your own.

Take Cyber Attack on Critical Service. The wizard walks through the scenario's drivers step by step. At each step, the reference assumptions from the MSTAR Bank are shown on the right; you enter your own figures on the left. Here, the probability of a cyber attack on each critical service --- internet banking, payments, card services, trading --- is set with a simple slider, against the reference values.

Once the drivers are set, the wizard runs the model and returns the result: an expected loss, an extreme loss, and the scenario's position on a frequency-severity grid. The figures are yours, computed from your inputs.

The whole thing takes a few minutes and needs no modelling. It gives a first quantified view for your bank, which you can later refine into a full model in MSTAR when the stakes justify it.

Try it yourself. A live scenario is available to test from the Conference Pack --- scan the QR code, pick a scenario, enter your own figures and see the result.

Build a scenario from scratch

We will start with a simplified Internal Fraud scenario, analysed using the XOI decomposition:

  • EXposure: each employee exposes the company to potential fraud.
  • Occurrence: the occurrence of the fraud is an individual, fairly rare event.
  • Impact: the impact is the total amount of the fraud before it is detected.

Starting with MSTAR

MSTAR is a desktop application. An MSTAR Project is a set of scenarios and additional elements such as risk indicators, what-if analyses, documentation, etc.

Within the project just created, we create the new model named "InternalFraud".

Designing the model structure

The first step in creating a model is to define its structure, i.e. the parameters which condition the main variables Exposure, Occurrence, Impact. A name and a label are attached to each node.

This model is based on the following analysis. Exposure at risk are employees and contractors. A loss occurs when a fraud is perpetrated. The probability of fraud depends on the seniority of the employee. The impact is equal to the product of:

  • The average amount of operations processed (potential fraud is higher for people dealing with high amounts).
  • An income factor depending on seniority (the potential fraud is higher for high income employees).
  • An intensity factor representing the number of operations that the fraudster could succeed to issue.

Now that the theoretical model is defined, we can create all the nodes in MSTAR in the same way.

Some variables are defined using Equations, some are defined using Dependency Tables. In that case, we have the formulas:

  • Exposure = Employees + Contractors
  • Impact = Income × Amount × Intensity

Green nodes Exposure, Occurrence and Impact must be defined using an equation.

The dependencies that are not defined using formulas are defined manually:

  • The probability of Fraud depends on Seniority.
  • The Income depends on Seniority.

Quantifying the model

Once all the nodes and dependencies are defined, the model is ready to be quantified. In the picture below, all nodes show a warning sign, meaning that the node is not yet quantified. The nodes need to be quantified top-down as dependencies exist.

We must define a quantification for each node. This is done by creating a quantifier for each node. When the structure does not change, revising a model requires only updating the quantifiers. This is why design and quantification are independent steps. This is also useful when using the same model for several Legal Entities.

Let's start with "Employees". The value of this node is 1000 in the low hypothesis, 1100 in the medium hypothesis, 1200 in the high hypothesis. This is a Numbered data type.

Continue with the other nodes "without parents". Nodes without parents (i.e. the root nodes of the graph) can be quantified directly. For nodes that have one or more parents, all parents must have been quantified first.

The "Fraud" quantifier is boolean (True/False) and depends on the seniority. The probability of fraud depends on the seniority. This is based on a statistical analysis of the observed cases, or on external data.

One more node needs to be quantified: Income, which is Numbered and also depends on level. To enter this index, a node state is defined for each possible value (1, 1.5 and 2) and a seniority is associated to the node state. This association is done by assigning a 100% probability to the value corresponding to the considered level.

Using the model

The model is now fully quantified. How to assess the average risk and the extreme risk? Every year, each employee can perpetrate a fraud or not. If this happens, the impact may vary. And the number of exposed employees is uncertain. The number of combinations is huge --- Monte-Carlo simulation can help evaluating them. There are no more warning icons on the graph, meaning that the model is ready for use.

When launching the simulation with 1 million iterations, you can observe:

  • The average risk (about $2M).
  • The extreme risk (about $25M).

The Monte Carlo simulation can "play" a very large number of possible situations by drawing random variables. It therefore allows to evaluate the distribution of possible situations.

Using the model --- What-if analysis

MSTAR can also help investigating mitigation actions. Employees taken into account are those who can perform the operations at risk. It is possible to reduce this number without impacting the production. But this requires an investment to better manage access rights. Investigating a mitigation action means comparing the required investment and the resulting risk reduction.

The what-if analysis will focus on the number of employees, on which we will make an alternative hypothesis. Call this new hypothesis "Mitigation", in addition to the default one. Enter the new hypothesis with respect to the number of employees. Creating a What-if analysis allows you to compare two alternatives much more quickly than by directly changing the quantifiers.

Launch the simulation, add the alternative "Mitigation" and re-run the simulation. Compare the costs: the extreme risk was significantly reduced. Before implementing the mitigation action, the probability of a loss greater than 12M€ was 5%; it is now reduced to 1%.

Conclusion

This example allowed us to understand how to model a risk using a structured assessment rather than a statistical model or a plain expert judgment. The advantage, of course, is to understand the risk and to be able to manage it. The example presented is relatively simple, but it clearly shows how risk mitigation can be addressed rationally.

MSTAR contributes to bridging the gap between risk measurement and risk management.

About us

Elseware develops methods and software for quantitative risk modelling.

Founded in 1993, our work began with early applications of neural networks to credit and market risk, before moving to Bayesian networks applied to the structured modelling of operational risk.

The XOI method — Exposure, Occurrence and Impact — was introduced in 2006. Since then, it has been developed through practical work with major banks and insurers across regulatory capital, economic capital, stress testing, operational resilience and risk management applications.

MSTAR is the software implementation of that approach. It combines explicit scenario structures, probabilistic modelling and Monte Carlo simulation with a growing body of reusable modelling knowledge and reference scenarios.

Our work has always followed the same principle: risk models should help explain how risk arises, not simply produce a number. That means making assumptions visible, linking quantification to the underlying business mechanism, and building models that can be challenged, reused and adapted as needs evolve.

MSTAR has helped industrialise and rationalise scenario construction. With the help of AI, we are now setting out to do the same for scenario challenge. By structuring scenarios around explicit loss-generation mechanisms, MSTAR made assumptions visible and quantification more systematic. We are now using AI to bring the same discipline to the challenge process: searching for evidence, confronting assumptions and documenting the reasoning, while keeping the process transparent, traceable and auditable.
